segments.text: Oceans cover most of Earth’s surface and strongly affect climate, transport, ecosystems and coastal life. This unit examines the shape of ocean basins, water properties, sea-floor sediments and the movement of ocean water.
Study it with one recurring question: what causes the pattern, and what effect does the pattern have? That approach works for temperature, salinity, currents, waves and tides.

items.text: Origin of oceans and seas

: Ocean basins developed through Earth’s geological evolution and plate tectonics, while ocean water accumulated over geological time through processes including outgassing and water cycling. For examination purposes, connect basin origin to crustal and tectonic development.
Ocean-basin features
: Major features include continental shelf, continental slope, abyssal plains, mid-ocean ridges, trenches and seamounts. Their distribution reflects crust type and plate processes.
Ocean temperature

: Sea-surface temperature varies mainly with latitude, season, currents, cloud and mixing. Temperature generally declines with depth through a thermocline in many regions before becoming cold and relatively stable in deep water.
Salinity
: Salinity reflects the balance among evaporation, precipitation, river inflow, ice processes and mixing. High evaporation can raise salinity; heavy rainfall or river input can lower it.
Ocean-floor deposits

: Marine sediments can originate from land, biological remains, chemical precipitation or very fine particles. Their distribution depends on distance from land, productivity, depth and ocean processes.
Ocean circulation
: Surface currents are strongly driven by winds and modified by Earth’s rotation and continents. Deep circulation is strongly influenced by density differences related to temperature and salinity.
Waves
: Most surface waves are generated by wind. Wave energy reshapes coasts through erosion and deposition, and wave behaviour changes as water becomes shallow near shore.
Currents
: Currents transport heat, nutrients and organisms and influence regional climate. Wind-driven surface circulation and density-driven deep circulation operate at different scales.
Tides

: Tides are periodic changes in sea level caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun together with Earth–Moon dynamics. Spring tides have larger tidal ranges; neap tides have smaller ranges.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

items.text: Continental shelf
: The shelf is a relatively shallow, gently sloping submerged extension of continental crust. Width varies greatly depending on tectonic setting and sediment supply.
Continental slope and rise

: The slope descends more steeply toward deep ocean basins. Sediment can move downslope through turbidity currents and other gravity-driven processes, building continental rises where tectonic conditions permit.
Abyssal plains
: Very flat deep-ocean regions are mantled by fine sediment. Their smoothness partly reflects sediment burial of rough underlying relief.
Mid-ocean ridges
: Ridges are divergent plate boundaries where new oceanic crust forms. Hydrothermal circulation and volcanic activity are common.
Trenches
: Deep trenches mark many subduction zones where oceanic lithosphere bends and descends beneath another plate.
Surface temperature
: Latitude is the broadest control, but currents, seasons, cloud, mixing and upwelling create major regional departures from simple latitudinal belts.
Thermocline
: In many low- and mid-latitude oceans, temperature decreases rapidly through an intermediate layer called the thermocline before becoming cold and relatively uniform at depth.
Salinity

: Average open-ocean salinity is about 35 practical salinity units, but regional values vary. Evaporation raises salinity, while precipitation, river inflow and ice melt tend to lower it; sea-ice formation can increase salinity of remaining water.
Density
: Colder and saltier seawater is generally denser. Density differences are central to vertical stratification and deep circulation.
Terrigenous sediment
: Material eroded from land reaches the ocean by rivers, wind, glaciers and coastal erosion. It is especially important near continents.
Biogenous sediment
: Shells and microscopic remains accumulate where biological production and preservation are sufficient. Calcium carbonate and silica are major components.
Hydrogenous sediment
: Some minerals precipitate directly from seawater or form through chemical processes on the sea floor.
Productivity
: Marine biological productivity is strongly affected by light and nutrient availability. Upwelling regions can be highly productive because deep nutrient-rich water reaches the surface.
Wind-driven gyres

: Prevailing winds, Coriolis deflection and continental boundaries organize large rotating surface-current systems. Western boundary currents such as the Gulf Stream are often narrow and fast; eastern boundary currents are broader and generally cooler.
Ekman transport

: Because Coriolis deflects moving water and friction transfers momentum downward, the net movement of the surface layer is at an angle to the wind. This helps explain coastal upwelling and downwelling.
Thermohaline circulation
: Deep circulation is driven by density differences associated with temperature and salinity. Dense water forms in some high-latitude regions and contributes to slow global overturning circulation.
Climate influence

: Currents redistribute heat and therefore affect coastal climate, sea ice, marine ecosystems and weather patterns. They interact with the atmosphere rather than acting as an independent climate system.
Wind waves

: Most ordinary surface waves form when wind transfers energy to water. Water particles mainly move in orbital paths while energy travels; the entire body of water does not move forward at wave speed.
Breaking waves
: As waves enter shallow water, friction slows the lower part of the wave, wavelength shortens and height can increase until the wave becomes unstable and breaks.
Tides
: Tides are very long-period waves caused mainly by the gravitational interaction of Earth, Moon and Sun. Local coastline and basin shape strongly modify the actual timing and range.
Spring tides
: When Sun, Moon and Earth are approximately aligned at new and full moon, lunar and solar tidal effects reinforce one another, producing larger tidal ranges.
Neap tides
: Near first and third quarter moon, solar and lunar effects partly offset one another, producing smaller tidal ranges.
Currents
: Currents are horizontal water movements driven by wind, density differences and tides. A tide is not simply another name for a current, although tides can generate tidal currents.

items.text: Draw a cross-section of an ocean basin.
Prepare separate diagrams for waves, currents and tides; never mix their definitions.
Make a salinity control table: process → raises/lowers salinity → example setting.
Use one example of a warm current and one cold current only if you can locate them correctly on a map.

rows: Avoid this error A tide is a periodic rise and fall of sea level; a current is horizontal movement of water; a wave mainly transmits energy. Keep these three concepts separate.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Explain basin origin and relief, then temperature/salinity, deposits, circulation, and finally compare waves, currents and tides with causes and effects.
• Federal Public Service Commission, Revised Scheme and Syllabus for CSS Competitive Examination (CE-2016 and onwards).
• NOAA National Ocean Service, resources on tides and currents (updated 2024).
• Ocean basins have distinct tectonic and sedimentary features.
• Temperature and salinity affect density and circulation.
• Surface currents are driven largely by wind; deep circulation is strongly density-related.
• Tides are not the same as waves or currents.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
